question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: A branch fell onto the porch, and I heard this sharp crack just overhead. That scared me. I remember the splinters beside the porch swing—that’s the bit that stays with me.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember losing sight of my nephew at the beach. There was a crowd blocking my view of the water, and I couldn’t see where he was. His red bucket was beside my chair, but he wasn’t there. I remember feeling really frightened, looking for him and not knowing where to look first. Mostly, what stays with me is that feeling of needing to see him and not being able to.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer:
One time I felt really proud was when a magazine accepted a poem I’d written. They mailed me a copy of the issue, and seeing the poem actually printed felt different from just knowing it had been accepted. My name was right there beneath the title. I kept looking at that part—my own name attached to something I’d made.

I work as a cashier in a college cafeteria, so having something I’d written appear in a magazine felt like a different side of me getting noticed. Someone had read it and wanted other people to read it, too. That meant a lot. I don’t remember all the details of what was happening around me, but I remember looking at the page and thinking, “I really did this.”

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I go to tennis practice every week. Head north from my home along Laurel Street, then turn left onto Court Lane at the gas station. It’s at number 48.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I felt sad when my sister moved to another country. Her suitcases were packed before the weekend, but it really hit me when we had one last breakfast together at the station. I was thinking about how far away she’d be.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had a bowl of rice porridge this morning, with sliced scallions stirred through it. It was breakfast before my early shift at the map shop. Nothing much stands out beyond that.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: One time, there was a split trash bag outside the garage, with fish scraps scattered over the pavement. Flies were circling the open bag. It was the combination of the exposed fish scraps and the flies that disgusted me. I just kept looking at that mess and thinking how nasty it was.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d probably give directions to my usual hardware store. Head north from my home along King Street, then turn left onto Laurel Road at the flower shop. The store is at 17 Laurel Road. That’s how I’d explain it—the flower shop is the landmark to look for.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember a foul puddle in a public shower, with a clump of hair across the drain. The gray suds were pooling around my sandals—that really disgusted me. Once I noticed the hair, it was hard to look at anything else.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d give directions to the public library, since I go there twice a week. From my home, head west along Cedar Lane. Look for the fountain—the library is on the right, opposite it. I’d point out the fountain as the landmark to watch for.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: “After breakfast I usually sweep the patio. I keep a short broom outside the door, so I get that and sweep the crumbs together, then tip them into the compost bin. It’s a little job I do each morning. There isn’t much of a story to it, really, but that’s the part of my morning that comes to mind—finishing breakfast, going outside, and getting the patio swept.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: “I remember a foul puddle in a public shower. There was a clump of hair across the drain, and gray suds were pooling around my sandals. The hair really disgusted me, but then I noticed the suds around my feet, and that felt worse—it wasn’t just something over by the drain. I kept looking between the clump of hair and the water around my sandals. Just the thought of standing in that puddle made me want to get away from it.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer:
“One time my car skidded on a patch of ice. What I remember most is a mailbox inches from my window. It was so close—that’s the part that really sticks with me. But the rear wheels were sliding toward a ditch, too, so my attention kept going between the mailbox and where the back of the car was going. I was afraid I couldn’t stop it going farther.

It’s strange what you remember, because I can picture that mailbox much more clearly than the rest of the road. I can’t give you every detail about who was around. Mostly I remember the car sliding and how little room there seemed to be.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I remember spilling coffee on a book I’d borrowed, with the owner sitting right across the table from me. It left a brown ring across the title page. I felt so careless—it was someone else’s book, and they were right there watching it happen. That’s what stands out most, the embarrassment of damaging something they’d trusted me with.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember a split trash bag outside the garage, with fish scraps scattered over the pavement. Flies were circling the open bag. Seeing all that made me feel disgusted—I just wanted to get away from it.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I misspelled a name on a birthday cake once. I’d put an extra letter in the icing, and the birthday boy was the one who spotted it. That was the embarrassing part—he noticed his own name was wrong before I did. I looked at it again, and then the extra letter seemed so obvious. Names are funny that way, you can look right at one and think it looks fine, and then once you see the mistake, it’s all you can see. I’d wanted it to look nice for him, and instead there was this mistake right on the cake. I felt very awkward about that.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: “I go to the public garden every week. Head east along Pine Road, then turn right onto Linden Street at the bakery. The garden’s at number 62. Linden makes me think of trees, and then I start thinking about the sky—I’m an amateur stargazer.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer:
I remember being by my garden chair with wasps swarming right beside it. There was a nest inside a hollow stump, and having so many of them that close was frightening. I was trying to keep track of where they were, but then one landed on my shirt collar.

That was the part that really scared me. It was so close to my neck, and I didn’t know whether moving would make it sting me. I wanted to get away, but I was afraid to make a sudden movement. My attention narrowed down to that one wasp on my collar, even with all the others flying nearby.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: I usually have coffee and work on the crossword, with the newspaper spread across the counter. I use a pencil with a pretty worn eraser. It’s a familiar way to start the morning.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember seeing a split trash bag outside the garage. There were fish scraps scattered over the pavement, and flies were circling the open bag. That was what really disgusted me—the fish lying out in the open with the flies around it. My attention kept going between the torn bag and the scraps on the ground. I didn’t want to get close to any of it. I was thinking what an unpleasant mess it was and how horrible it would be to have to pick it all up.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember a tipped-over compost pail with maggots underneath it. That was what disgusted me—the maggots, and then noticing the rotting peaches stuck to the rim. The peaches made the whole thing seem even worse. The lid was wedged against the fence, so it wasn’t covering any of it. It’s funny which details stay with you: I picture that lid against the fence, but then my attention goes straight back to what was underneath the pail. Just thinking about that makes me feel disgusted again.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember making pancake batter when a rotten egg spoiled it. There was this sulfur smell all through the kitchen and watery, greenish liquid in the bowl. It was really disgusting.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: I remember being at a street fair with my niece. There was an accordion player, and she invited me to dance. She was teaching me the polka, and I just enjoyed being there with her. That’s what stands out most—the music and the happiness of dancing together.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I felt sad on my last visit to my childhood home. There were pale squares on the walls where the family photos had hung, and I remember the key left on the counter. It was still familiar, but it didn’t feel quite like home anymore. What stayed with me was the feeling of saying goodbye to a part of my life.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had a beet and goat cheese salad for dinner, with toasted walnuts scattered over the beets. The walnuts stand out in my memory—the crunch, compared with the soft cheese. And the beets have quite a strong color, so that’s the first picture that comes to mind when I think about it. I also had a slice of buttered rye on the side. Rye has that distinctive taste of its own. I remember the food more clearly than what I was thinking about while I ate.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I remember making an introduction at the front door and suddenly forgetting my dinner guest’s name. I knew who she was, but when I needed to say her name, it just wouldn’t come to me. She quietly supplied it herself. That was the embarrassing part—having to have my own guest help me introduce her. I wanted to make her feel welcome, and instead I was standing there unable to remember something so basic.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d give them directions to the bowling alley, since I go there every week. From my home, head west along Cooper Avenue. The bowling alley is on the right, beside the laundromat. I’d tell them to look for the laundromat as a landmark.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: I feed the sparrows before breakfast, scoop the sunflower seeds out of the tin, and put fresh water in the birdbath. Water always makes me think of the pool—I work as a swimming pool caretaker.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud when I made my first batch of homemade dumplings. I used ginger in the pork filling and got the pleats fairly even. It felt good to make them myself.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: For supper I had chickpea stew over brown rice. There were carrots diced into the stew, and a pinch of cumin stirred into the broth.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember finding a slug inside a head of lettuce. There was a slick trail across the leaves and grit between the inner folds. It all felt dirty and slimy, and it really put me off the lettuce.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I felt sad when an old pear tree was cut down. There was a split running through the trunk, and the tire swing was left on the grass. That’s the part I remember most—the tree gone and the swing lying there. It all felt rather empty.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: “Before breakfast, I feed the sparrows. I scoop the sunflower seeds out of a tin, and I pour fresh water into the birdbath. The water makes me think of my work—I’m a swimming pool caretaker. A birdbath is a rather different size of thing, but there’s water to look after there, too. Feeding the sparrows is something I do every morning.”

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: After breakfast each morning, I sweep the patio. I keep a short broom outside the door, so I get that and sweep up the crumbs, then tip them into the compost bin. That’s a regular part of my morning.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud when I sang my first solo at choir practice. It was a folk song we were rehearsing, and I remember coming in cleanly on the high note. That’s the part that stands out to me—not so much everything around it, but the feeling of getting it right. It felt like a real accomplishment.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: I remember winning two concert seats in a raffle. My favorite quartet was on the program, so I was really pleased. My cousin was free to come with me, which made it even nicer. It was the lovely feeling of having something to look forward to and someone to share it with. I don’t remember all the little details, but I remember being very happy about it.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: “I usually do a crossword puzzle over coffee in the morning. I have the newspaper spread across the counter and use a pencil with a worn eraser. That’s my usual morning routine—coffee and the crossword.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember finding a dead mouse in a watering can. There was this rancid smell coming from inside, and its tail was sticking out of the spout. It really turned my stomach.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember seeing a cockroach inside a bakery display case. Then I noticed a second one underneath a pastry tray. That was bad enough, but one of them was brushing a glazed bun with its antennae. That’s the part that really disgusted me—the contact with something people were going to eat. I kept looking at the bun and the roach, and the pastries just didn’t look appetizing anymore.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d give them directions to the municipal pool, where I go for my regular swim. Head south from my home along Willow Avenue. The pool is on the right, just past the firehouse.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I remember the first time I went fishing after my friend died. His usual seat in the boat was empty, and seeing it like that made me miss him. His initials were on the tackle box, too. Those familiar things felt different without him there. I was fishing, but mostly I was thinking about how he wasn’t going to be there with me again.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: “When my missing cat came home. That’s a happy memory. I remember the muddy paw prints on the porch, and that familiar bell on the collar. It’s such a little sound, but when it’s your cat, it means something. And the muddy prints—usually you think about the mess, but those were lovely to see. My cat was home. That was what mattered.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I stepped in dog droppings on the sidewalk once. There was this brown smear across my shoe, and the smell followed me onto the bus. That was the worst part, not being able to get away from it.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer:
I remember a neighbor being snowed in after a storm. There was a deep drift against her front steps, and it struck me how difficult it would be for her just to get out. What looked like a lot of snow to me was really an obstacle for her.

I shoveled a path to her gate. I remember looking at the snow and thinking that clearing even that stretch was something practical I could do. I felt sorry that she was stuck like that, but I wanted to do more than just feel sorry. That’s the part that stays with me—being able to help with what was right in front of me.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I felt sad saying goodbye to my longtime upstairs neighbor when she was moving away. We had a final coffee together on the landing, with her moving boxes beside the stairwell. Those boxes are something I remember clearly. She’d been upstairs for so long, and there we were having coffee knowing it was the last time before she left. I was thinking about how strange it would feel not having her living above me anymore. I was glad we had that time together, but I didn’t want to say goodbye.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had beef tacos for lunch today, in a paper tray from the food truck. There were thin slices of radish over the beef.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had a beet and goat cheese salad for dinner, with toasted walnuts scattered over the beets. There was a slice of buttered rye on the side, too.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer:
I run a kiosk on a ferry pier, and one time a delivery cyclist was stranded there after dark. They had a flat tire on the rear wheel. I felt sorry for them—being stuck with a bike is awkward enough, but in the dark it seemed that much harder to deal with.

I had a work light, so I lent it to them. It wasn’t going to fix the tire, but at least they’d have some light to see what they were doing. I wanted to make things a little easier for them.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember being at supper with an exchange student who was homesick. He had a photograph of his family beside his plate, and I felt sorry for him being so far from them. I lent him my phone so he could call home. I remember wanting to help him feel a little less alone. It wasn’t a big thing to do, but it felt like something I could offer.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember a moth floating in my tea. Its tiny legs were brushing the rim of the cup, and its wet wings were against the teaspoon. The whole thing looked so unpleasant. It really put me off the tea.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I misspelled the birthday boy’s name on a cake once—put an extra letter in the icing. And he was the one who spotted it, which was the embarrassing part. His own name, on his birthday cake, and I’d got it wrong. One extra letter sounds like such a little thing, but it doesn’t feel little when it’s someone’s name.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember a dog charging toward me across a driveway, with its broken tether dragging behind it. There was a low gate between us, but I still felt really scared. It all happened so quickly.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: I usually shave before I have my shower. I use a shaving brush with warm lather, and there’s a small mirror above the basin that I shave in front of. That’s a regular part of my morning.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud when I finished my first quilt for my niece. The corners lined up evenly, and I’d stitched her initials into one square. That little square is what I remember most—it made the quilt feel like it was really hers.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: “I grind coffee by hand each morning. The grinder’s clamped to the kitchen counter, and I keep the beans in a blue tin. That’s where I’d start describing my morning—the blue tin, then the grinder. It’s the part I do every morning.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer:
I felt sad at the last screening at the neighborhood cinema. There was a western on that evening. What stays with me isn’t so much the story of the film as the thought that this was the last screening. I’d try to pay attention to the western, and then I’d be thinking about that again. It made the whole thing feel different.

I kept the ticket stub. It’s only a little piece of paper, but throwing it away felt different from throwing away an ordinary ticket. That sounds funny coming from me—I work as a supply clerk at an aquarium shop, so I’m used to thinking about things in a practical way. But that wasn’t practical, really. I just wanted to keep something from it. I still have it.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had mushroom risotto for dinner last night, with peas folded into the rice and grated Parmesan sprinkled on top. The Parmesan is the first thing that comes to mind, then the peas mixed through it. Peas make me think of little planets, actually—I’m an amateur stargazer, so my mind goes that way. But yes, mushroom risotto was my last meal.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer:
“The last screening at the neighborhood cinema comes to mind. There was a western on that evening, but when I think back to it, it’s the cinema I think about more than the film. It was the last screening—that was the sad part. A film ends, but this felt like an ending beyond the film, too.

I kept the ticket stub. A ticket is usually just something you use to get in, isn’t it? But I still have that last one. It makes me think of the place.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: “A gym towel in a locker comes to mind. It smelled of mildew, and it was sitting there in these damp folds. That dampness was what really disgusted me—then I noticed the dark blotches along the hem, and that made it worse. Once I’d noticed those, the smell seemed even more unpleasant. I work as a swimming pool caretaker, so a wet towel itself isn’t strange to me, but this was different: that musty smell and the blotches together. I really didn’t want to touch it.”

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: I usually grind coffee by hand. The grinder’s clamped to the kitchen counter, and I keep the beans in a blue tin. That’s what comes to mind first—the tin, then turning the handle.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember a dog charging toward me across a driveway. Its tether had snapped and was dragging behind it. There was a low gate between us, but I felt very afraid seeing it coming at me like that. That’s what stands out—the dog rushing toward me and the gate not seeming like much of a barrier.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: “I’d tell them to head west from my home along Harbor Road. I go to the music store regularly, so that’s the place I’d use. It’s on the right, opposite the fountain. I’d probably mention the fountain first, actually—it’s something to look for rather than just trying to remember which side the shop is on. Fountains make me think about work, too, because I’m a swimming pool caretaker, although that doesn’t help much with the directions. Anyway, west along Harbor Road, then look for the music store on your right, across from the fountain.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer:
I remember looking down in a public shower and seeing this foul puddle around my sandals. There were gray suds pooling there, and then I noticed a clump of hair stretched across the drain. That was the part that really disgusted me—the hair caught there, with all that water around it.

You go into a shower thinking about getting clean, and suddenly all I could think about was what I was standing in. My sandals didn’t feel like much of a barrier once I started looking at the suds around them. And then my attention kept going back to the drain. I wished I hadn’t looked so closely, but once I’d seen the hair, it was hard not to keep noticing it.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d give them directions to the rowing club, where I go regularly for practice. Head south from my home along Mill Street. The clubhouse is on the left, opposite the boat ramp.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d tell them to head north along Elm Avenue, then turn right onto Mill Road by the clock tower. The Saturday farmers market is at 35 Mill Road.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I remember visiting my childhood home for the last time. It felt strange seeing it so empty. There were pale squares on the walls where the family photos had hung, and those little traces made me sad. The house was still familiar, but it didn’t feel quite like home anymore. I remember the key left on the counter. There was a sense of something being over, and of not quite wanting to leave.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer:
I remember being inside a cave when my flashlight went out. The entrance was hidden around a bend, so I didn’t even have that opening to look toward. That was what frightened me—being inside and not being able to see the way out.

There was cold water dripping onto my shoulders. It’s funny what stands out: that cold feeling is really clear in my memory. I work as a swimming pool caretaker, so water is familiar, but it felt very different there, in the dark. My attention kept going between the water on my shoulders and that bend hiding the entrance.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: “I remember a neighbor unpacking groceries with one hand because her baby was asleep in her other arm. My attention went to the baby first, and then I noticed the heavy jars she was trying to put away. It struck me how awkward that was—having something you need to get done while you’re holding someone who needs you. I felt for her. I helped put the heavy jars away. It was a small thing, but watching her manage everything one-handed made me want to take a little of the work off her.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer:
“The first quilt I finished for my niece—that’s something I felt proud of. Her initials were stitched into one square, and I remember looking at those and thinking, that makes it hers. It wasn’t just a quilt I’d finished; it was for her.

And the corners lined up evenly. That probably sounds like a little thing, but your eye goes straight to where the pieces meet. Well, mine does. I kept looking at that, then back at her initials, and then trying to take in the whole quilt instead of just the separate squares.

I work as a cashier at a lighting store, and this was a different sort of satisfaction—having something finished that I could look at and say, ‘I made that.’ That’s the part I remember most.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud when I sang my first solo at choir practice. It was a folk song we were rehearsing, and I remember coming in cleanly on the high note. That’s the part that stands out most. It felt good to hear my own voice carrying that bit of the song and know I’d got it right.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I stepped in dog droppings on the sidewalk, and there was this brown smear across my shoe. Just looking at it made me feel sick, but the smell was worse. It followed me onto the bus—that’s the part I really remember. You leave the mess behind on the pavement, but you haven’t actually left it behind because it’s on your shoe. I kept noticing that smell and thinking about what I’d stepped in. Ugh.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer:
I remember a neighbor being snowed in after a storm. There was a deep drift against her front steps, and I felt for her, thinking about having all that snow in the way just to get out of the house.

I shoveled a path to her gate. What was on my mind was making it a little easier for her—something I could actually do, rather than just feel bad about her being snowed in. That’s the occasion that comes to mind.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud when my homemade kite finally stayed up in the air. I’d made a longer tail for it, cut from an old sheet. What I remember most is seeing it above the dunes and realizing it was actually staying aloft. It was up there for ten minutes. That might not sound like much, but it was something I’d made myself, and there it was, flying. That was the part I felt proud of.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: “I was happy when I picked my first balcony strawberries. Six ripe berries, all in one bowl. I saved two for a neighbor—I wanted to share them, though I was pleased just looking at what I’d grown.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud when my homemade kite finally stayed up. I’d added a longer tail cut from an old sheet, and it flew above the dunes for ten minutes. It felt good to see something I’d made actually work.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d probably give them directions to my weekly tennis practice, at 48 Court Lane. From my home, you head north along Laurel Street. Then, when you get to the gas station, turn left onto Court Lane. The gas station is the landmark I’d tell them to look for, and then they’d want number 48.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer:
I felt proud of a serving bowl I made on the pottery wheel. What I remember most is how it looked after firing—the blue glaze covering the inside and the smooth rim. Those are the details that stand out to me, rather than who was around.

It was satisfying to look at it and think, “I made that.” It wasn’t just the idea of a bowl anymore; it was an actual serving bowl, something I’d made myself. The smooth rim was a big part of it. I could look at the finished piece and feel pleased with how it had turned out. It was a quiet sort of pride.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: The last meal I ate was lunch today. I had a grilled cheese sandwich with thin slices of tomato inside and a dill pickle on the side.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: The last meal I had was supper—pan-fried cod and boiled potatoes. My brother was sitting across the table from me. I put a squeeze of lemon over the fish. That’s what I remember most clearly: the food and my brother there opposite me. I don’t remember exactly what we were talking about or what was on my mind.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I felt sad when an old pear tree was cut down. There was a split running through its trunk. I remember the tire swing left on the grass—it felt strange seeing it there without the tree.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I go to the municipal pool regularly to swim. Head south from my home along Willow Avenue. The pool is on the right, just past the firehouse.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud when the council voted to build the picnic shelter I’d proposed. I’d presented a sketch at a town meeting, and it felt good to know my idea was going to happen.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I remember feeling sad when my father missed my school play. His train was delayed by snow, so he couldn’t get there. I’d saved a program for him and had really wanted him to see it.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: I usually listen to the weather on the local station on my kitchen radio. I lace up my boots while the forecast is on, getting ready for work at the tent rental counter.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember finding a spoiled orange in a lunch bag. It had green fuzz around the stem, and the sour juice had soaked into the cloth lining. That was the worst part—the mess wasn’t just on the orange anymore. The whole thing was really disgusting.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember losing sight of my nephew at the beach. There was a crowd blocking my view of the water, and I couldn’t see where he was. His red bucket was beside my chair, but he wasn’t in sight. I felt really afraid—not knowing where he was was the worst part.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: I remember being at a street fair with my niece. There was an accordion player, and she invited me to dance. She was teaching me the polka, and it was just a happy time being there with her. What I remember most is the music and how much I enjoyed doing something together.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer:
“I remember stepping in dog droppings on the sidewalk. There was this brown smear across my shoe, and just looking at it made me feel sick. It’s that feeling of something filthy being on you—even though it was on my shoe, I didn’t want to touch anything near it.

Then the smell followed me onto the bus. That’s the part that really sticks with me, because getting away from the spot didn’t get me away from it. My attention kept going back to my shoe, then to the smell, then to wondering whether anyone else could smell it. I couldn’t tell you who was there specifically. I was too caught up in it. All I wanted was to get it off, but I didn’t want to have to deal with cleaning it either.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer:
I remember my grandson riding his bike without help for the first time. We were in the courtyard, and his father was on the steps filming him. He managed a full lap around the courtyard on his own. I kept watching him go, waiting to see if he could make it all the way around, and he did.

That made me so happy. It was such a simple thing, watching him ride a bike, but it felt like a big moment. I was proud of him, and I was glad his father was filming so we could have that moment to look back on.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: “I felt proud of a serving bowl I made on the pottery wheel. It had blue glaze covering the inside, and after it was fired, the rim was smooth. Those are the details I remember most—the blue inside and how smooth that edge was. Looking at the finished bowl and thinking, ‘I made that,’ felt really good.”

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: The last meal I ate was lentil soup for lunch today. I had it during a short break between classes, with some warm flatbread folded beside the bowl.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: “I remember a tipped compost pail, with maggots underneath. There were rotting peaches stuck to the rim, and the lid was wedged against the fence. Just looking at it made me feel sick.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: One time I was in an elevator and it stalled between two floors. The lights dimmed for a moment, and that was frightening—not knowing what was happening or how I was going to get out. My attention was on the elevator and whether it would move again. A guard answered the emergency intercom, so I had someone to speak to, but being stuck between floors was what scared me.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I remember feeling sad when an old pear tree was cut down. There was a split running through the trunk, but it was still sad to see it gone. The tire swing was left on the grass, and that’s the part I remember most. Everything felt a little empty without the tree there.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I misspelled a name on a birthday cake—put an extra letter in the icing. The birthday boy spotted it. I felt embarrassed, especially since it was his own name. That’s the bit I remember most.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer:
“I usually loosen up before I go for my walk. I do slow shoulder rolls by the window, just taking my time with them. Being by the window gets me looking outside, and then I’m thinking about the sky rather than counting the rolls. I’m an amateur stargazer, so the sky tends to catch my attention.

“I also do calf stretches at the kitchen counter. The counter gives me something to hold on to while I stretch. Those are the main things I do before the walk—the shoulder rolls by the window and the calf stretches in the kitchen. I like to get loosened up first rather than go straight out.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: My first win at the chess club comes to mind. The game lasted nearly an hour, and I finally got checkmate with my last rook. That’s the part I feel proudest of—my last rook, and it was enough. Nearly an hour is a long time to stay with a game. I’m an amateur stargazer, and that makes me think of looking for something in the sky, how one small thing can hold your attention. But yes, that checkmate—that was a proud moment for me.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember a moth floating in my tea. Its tiny legs were brushing the rim of the cup, and its wet wings were against the teaspoon. It was such an unpleasant sight—the whole cup seemed dirty to me after that.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer:
“I remember returning a library book that was years late. I was at the library, and the librarian unfolded my old checkout slip. That little bit of paper made me feel more embarrassed than handing over the book had. Then there was the due date stamped inside the cover—it’s one thing to know you’re late, and another to see the actual date sitting there.

“I kept wondering what the librarian thought of me. I can’t say what they actually thought, but I felt very conspicuous. I wanted to explain, except I didn’t have an explanation that would make it less late. Dates are funny—I enjoy looking up at stars and thinking about enormous stretches of time, but that small stamped date was quite enough time for me to think about just then.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer:
I felt sad when my old school was being demolished. I remember the bell being lowered from the tower. It looked different down there—when it was up in the tower, you hardly thought about it as an actual thing that could be taken away.

There were chalkboards piled beside the front gate, too. Those stayed in my mind. A gate is where you come and go, and there were all these things that belonged inside, sitting beside it. I kept looking from the boards to the tower.

It made me think about how a place can still be so familiar to you even when you don’t go there anymore. I hadn’t really thought of losing it before. Then, seeing it being taken apart, I felt that I was losing something I couldn’t put back.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember seeing a passenger struggling with a heavy suitcase. The luggage rack was too high for her to reach, and I felt for her, trying to manage it on her own. I helped lift the suitcase onto the rack. It was a small thing, but I wanted to make it easier for her.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember being far from shore in a canoe when a sudden gust came from behind and it overturned. One paddle was drifting out of reach. I felt afraid, thinking about how far I was from shore.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer:
“I remember taking a turn out of order when I was bowling. The person who was supposed to go next was still choosing a ball, and I went ahead as though it was my turn. And I got a strike, which sounds like the good part, except it went up under the wrong name.

I was looking at the score, expecting to see it next to my name, and that was when it clicked. Then I looked over and the next bowler was still choosing a ball. There are so many balls to choose from—you pick one up and it doesn’t feel right, so you try another. But that doesn’t mean they’ve given up their turn.

That was the embarrassing part. I’d been pleased with myself for the strike, and then suddenly I just felt foolish. It wasn’t even my turn to be pleased about.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember a tourist who had missed the last bus. She was by the curb with two heavy suitcases, and I felt sorry for her, being stuck there with all that luggage. I gave her a ride to her hotel. It seemed like a simple thing I could do to help.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: I usually tend to my two window boxes in the morning. I get water from the kitchen tap and pinch off the spent geranium blooms. It’s a quiet little routine.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer:
One time my canoe overturned when I was far from shore. I remember a sudden gust coming from behind, and then the canoe tipping over. It happened so quickly that I didn’t have much time to think before I was in the water.

One paddle was drifting out of reach. That really frightened me—seeing it move away and knowing how far I was from shore. My attention kept going between the canoe, the paddle, and the shore. I wanted to get hold of the paddle, but I was afraid of getting farther from the canoe. I remember that uncertainty most clearly, not knowing what to do first.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud when I painted a mural for a playground—three blue whales along the wall. A kindergarten class was there for the unveiling. It felt good to have made something for them.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: “On weekdays I have breakfast at the kitchen counter. I have rye bread, toasted on one side, and black tea in a green mug. The bread is toasted on just the one side, not both. When I picture the morning, it’s mostly that bit I remember—the counter, the toast, the green mug. That gets me thinking about work, too. I’m a supply clerk at an aquarium shop, so my mind can go from breakfast to the shop. But breakfast at the counter is the clearest part of the routine to describe.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud of a mural I painted for a playground. It had three blue whales along the wall. There was a kindergarten class at the unveiling, and I remember feeling pleased to see something I’d painted become part of a place for children. It was nice to stand there and think, “I made that.” That’s what stays with me more than the details of the day.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: “I’d give them directions to the public garden at 62 Linden Street. I go there every week. From my home, you head east along Pine Road, then turn right onto Linden Street at the bakery. The bakery is the landmark I’d tell them to look for, and then the address they want is number 62—the public garden.”

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: On weekday mornings, I usually take my terrier for a loop around the block. When we get back, I refill the dog’s water bowl. That’s the usual routine.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer:
I felt proud when the council voted to build a picnic shelter I’d proposed. I’d presented a sketch at a town meeting, so it wasn’t just something I’d been thinking about privately anymore. I was putting the idea in front of other people and showing them what I had in mind.

What stands out most is that vote. There’s a difference between having an idea yourself and hearing that other people want to go ahead with it. I remember thinking, “They’re actually going to build it.” I felt pleased that I’d spoken up and that my sketch had helped turn the proposal into something people could picture.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I joined the wrong class at a dance studio. There were couples practicing a waltz around me, and I had my tap shoes in a drawstring bag. That’s the detail that sticks with me—the bag, with completely the wrong shoes inside. Everyone was moving in pairs, and there I was with my tap shoes. A waltz is so smooth, too, and tap makes me think of all that clattering. I felt embarrassed being in the middle of something I clearly hadn’t come for.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d send them east from my home along Alder Road, toward the bakery I usually go to. It’s on the left beside the laundromat—that’s the landmark I’d tell them to look for.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember finding a slug inside a head of lettuce. There was a slick trail across the leaves and grit between the inner folds. It really put me off—the whole thing felt dirty, especially finding that tucked inside. I don’t remember much about where I was or who was around, but I remember not wanting to touch it anymore.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I remember taking the wrong suitcase at baggage claim. Both bags had matching yellow straps, and I thought the one I picked up was mine. The other traveler was waiting right beside the carousel, which made it more embarrassing when I realized my mistake. I’d been so sure I had the right bag just because of that strap. Then there I was, with someone else’s suitcase, feeling foolish for not checking more carefully.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer:
I remember forgetting a dinner guest’s name during an introduction at the front door. I got to the point where I needed to say her name, and my mind just went blank. I knew I should know it, and the harder I tried to remember, the more awkward that pause felt.

She quietly supplied her name, which was kind of her. I was grateful she didn’t make a big thing of it, but I felt embarrassed. I wanted her to feel welcome, and instead I was standing there unable to remember something so basic.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I remember pushing on a glass door that was marked “pull.” My colleagues were watching from the lobby, and the receptionist ended up opening it for me. It was such a simple thing to get wrong, and I felt silly doing it in front of people I worked with.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer:
I remember taking the wrong suitcase at baggage claim. I was beside the carousel, looking for my bag, and I saw one with a yellow strap like mine. I took it, thinking it was mine, but both bags had matching yellow straps. The other traveler was still waiting beside the carousel, and I’d picked up their suitcase.

That was the embarrassing part—realizing I’d been so sure just because of the strap. I hadn’t checked carefully enough. I keep track of stock at a bookstore, so I’m used to paying attention to which thing is which. It felt silly to get my own luggage wrong. I was mostly thinking about getting the bag back to the right person and wishing I’d looked more closely before taking it.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I felt sad when a family photograph was ruined in a flood. I remember it drying on a towel, and the stain across my father’s picture. I kept looking at that part, then at the rest of the photograph.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I go to the bowling alley every week. From my home, you head west along Cooper Avenue. The bowling alley is on the right, beside the laundromat.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: “I’d give them directions to the public library, since I go there twice a week. Head west from my home along Cedar Lane. The library is on the right, opposite the fountain—that’s the landmark I’d tell them to look for.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I felt sad saying goodbye to my foster dog. Its blanket was folded by the front door, and the new owner’s leash was on its collar. The blanket caught my eye—I kept thinking how quiet it would be without the dog there.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud the first time I finished a crossword without any help. It was a Sunday puzzle with a science theme, and I penciled in the last answer over breakfast. What stands out is the satisfaction of having worked it all out myself. It felt like a small thing, but a real accomplishment.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: “I’d probably send them to my usual grocery store, at 24 Birch Road. You head east from my home along Canal Street, then turn right onto Birch Road at the florist. The florist is the thing I’d tell them to look for—it’s easier to picture a shop than just remember a street name. Shops make me think of work, although I work at an aquarium shop, so that’s a different sort of shop. Anyway, Birch Road, number 24. That’s where the grocery store is.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: I remember feeling really happy when my raffle ticket won two concert seats. My favorite quartet was on the program, so it was something I really wanted to go to. My cousin was free to come with me, too. That made it even nicer—having someone to share it with. I remember feeling lucky and looking forward to it.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d give directions to my usual hardware store at 17 Laurel Road. Head north from my home along King Street, then turn left onto Laurel Road at the flower shop.

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d give them directions to the rowing club, where I go for practice. From my home, you head south along Mill Street. The clubhouse is on the left, opposite the boat ramp. That’s the main thing I’d tell them to look for.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer:
One time I felt really afraid was when an elevator I was in stalled between two floors. The lights dimmed for a moment, and I remember wondering whether it was going to drop. Not knowing what was happening was the worst part. I couldn’t tell whether it was just a brief interruption or whether I was stuck there.

A guard answered the emergency intercom. Hearing someone answer was reassuring, though I was still scared. At least someone knew I was there. My attention was really fixed on the elevator—whether the lights would change again, whether it would move. It was hard to think about anything else.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer:
I remember my neighbor trying to unpack her groceries with one hand because her baby was asleep in her other arm. My attention went to the baby at first, and then I noticed how much she was trying to manage without disturbing that sleep. Something as ordinary as putting groceries away looked like quite a job with only one hand.

I felt for her. There were heavy jars to put away, so I helped with those. It wasn’t a big thing on my part, but I kept thinking how different the same little task can be when your arms are already full. She could keep holding her baby, and I could take care of that bit.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had pan-fried cod and boiled potatoes for supper. My brother was across the table. I remember squeezing some lemon over the fish.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer:
“I grind coffee by hand each morning. The beans are in a blue tin, and the grinder’s clamped to the kitchen counter, so that’s where I stand to do it. It takes a little while, turning the handle. There’s something nice about having that one thing to do before getting caught up in the day.

“The blue tin is what comes to mind first when you ask, actually, even before the coffee. It’s funny how a color can make you picture a whole place. I work as a cashier at a lighting store, so that makes me think about how things look under different lights. But in the morning I’m not necessarily thinking about work. Sometimes it’s just the beans and turning the handle, and then my mind wanders. That’s the part of my morning I can picture most clearly.”

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: “I’d tell them how to get to the bakery, because that’s a trip I usually make. You head east from my home along Alder Road, and the bakery is on the left, beside the laundromat. I’d probably say to look for the laundromat as well, because sometimes it’s easier to find a place by what’s next to it. East isn’t always helpful if you’re not sure which way you’re facing. I work as a cashier at a lighting store, and that’s another place I could talk about, but the bakery is the one I was thinking of. On the left beside the laundromat—that’s what I’d want them to remember.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer:
I remember being in the kitchen making pancake batter and cracking a rotten egg into the mixing bowl. There was this sulfur smell that seemed to fill the whole kitchen. Looking into the bowl, I could see watery, greenish liquid mixed in with the batter. The sight of it and that smell together were really disgusting.

What bothered me was that I’d been making something to eat, and suddenly I couldn’t stand the thought of eating it. I kept looking at the bowl, thinking how horrible it was that one egg had spoiled the whole batter. The smell was the part that really stuck with me.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer:
One time that comes to mind is getting a birthday parcel from an old roommate. It was wrapped in a faded road map, which made it stand out. I remember looking at the wrapping before opening it—it was such a nice way to turn something ordinary into a present.

Inside was my favorite board game from childhood. That was the part that really made me happy. There’s something lovely about seeing something you used to love and having that feeling come back. And it wasn’t just the game; it was knowing my old roommate had thought of me. I don’t remember every detail of where I was when I opened it, but I remember feeling remembered.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer:
I remember a child dropping her ice cream. She still had the cone in her hand, but it was empty. That was the part that got to me—holding on to the cone when the thing she’d been enjoying was gone.

It might seem like a small disappointment to an adult, but I thought about how much something like that can matter when you’re little. I felt sorry for her, and there was something simple I could do, so I bought her a replacement scoop. I wanted her to have that little bit of enjoyment back.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: “I was happy when my missing cat came home. There were muddy paw prints on the porch, and that familiar bell on the collar… such a little sound, but it meant a lot.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember a moth floating in my tea, its tiny legs brushing the rim and wet wings against the teaspoon. It just made me feel sick looking at it.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember a gym towel in a locker, all folded up damp. The mildew smell was disgusting, and there were dark blotches along the hem. Just looking at those damp folds made me not want to touch it.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember a small earthquake during dinner. The overhead lamp was swinging sideways, and I could hear the plates rattling inside the cupboard. It was frightening to have things moving around like that. Those are the things that stand out most to me.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember opening a water bottle and noticing a sour smell under the cap. There was a slimy lining inside, and gray sludge clinging to the straw. It was really disgusting, especially seeing that stuff in something meant for drinking. That’s what sticks with me most—the smell and how slimy it looked.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I spilled coffee on a book I’d borrowed, with the owner sitting right across the table. It left a brown ring on the title page. I felt awkward about damaging something that wasn’t mine.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember finding a spoiled orange in my lunch bag. There was green fuzz around the stem, and sour juice had soaked into the cloth lining. It was just really unpleasant to look at and smell.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer:
I remember seeing a child searching for a lost mitten in the park. They had one bare hand tucked inside their sleeve, and that little detail made me feel for them. They were looking for something so small, but it mattered to them.

I helped check beneath the park benches. I wanted to do something useful rather than just feel sorry for them and walk past. It was a small thing to help with, but I remember feeling that they shouldn’t have to look all on their own.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer:
“I remember seeing a new classmate eating lunch alone. There was just one tray on his table, and that was what caught my eye. A single tray doesn’t usually mean much, but knowing he was new, I wondered whether he had anyone to sit with yet.

I was with my lunch group, and I thought about how different lunch must feel when you don’t know people. Everyone else seems to know where to go, who to sit beside. I didn’t know whether he actually wanted company, but I felt bad thinking he might be waiting for someone to ask. So I invited him to join us. I wanted him to know there was a place for him, without making a big thing of him being alone.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember a tourist who had missed the last bus. She was by the curb with two heavy suitcases, and I felt sorry for her, being somewhere unfamiliar with all that luggage. I gave her a ride to her hotel. I just thought how difficult it would be to be stuck like that, and I wanted to help.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember finding a slug inside a head of lettuce. There was a slick trail on the leaves and grit tucked into the folds. It really put me off touching it.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: I remember finding a dead mouse in a watering can. Its tail was sticking out of the spout, and there was this rancid smell coming from inside. That’s what really disgusted me—the smell, together with realizing what the little tail belonged to. It wasn’t just dirty water or something that needed rinsing out. There was a dead animal in there. I didn’t want to get close enough to look any more carefully. Even remembering it, it’s that combination of the tail and the smell that comes back to me.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember a passenger boarding the bus in sleet, gripping a metal walker with bare hands. I felt for them, being out in that weather without anything covering their hands. I had a spare pair of mittens, so I offered them. It was a small thing, but I wanted to help them feel a little warmer.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: My last meal was a bowl of rice porridge this morning, with sliced scallions stirred through it. It was breakfast before my early shift at the map shop, where I work as an assistant.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had beef tacos for lunch today from a food truck. They came in a paper tray, with thin slices of radish over the beef. Those are the main things I remember about it.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had mushroom risotto last night, with peas and grated Parmesan on top. The little peas made me think of planets scattered around.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember slipping on the basement stairs. A tread was loose beneath my heel, and I caught the rail with one hand. For a moment I was afraid I was going to fall.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember seeing a passenger struggling with a heavy suitcase. The luggage rack was too high for her to reach, and I felt for her, trying to manage it on her own. I helped lift the suitcase onto the rack. It was a small thing, but I wanted to make things a little easier for her.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: One time a falling branch struck the porch. There was this sharp crack just overhead—that’s what I remember first. Then the splinters beside the porch swing. A swing makes you think of somewhere to sit and relax, and then seeing those splinters right beside it… that frightened me. When I think back on it, I picture the swing, but it’s that crack overhead that really stays with me.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: I tend my two window boxes every morning. I get water from the kitchen tap and pinch off the spent geranium blooms. That’s a regular part of my morning, looking after those plants.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: I usually have the kitchen radio on the local station and listen to the weather forecast while I lace up my boots. That’s a regular part of my morning, getting ready for work. I work at a tent rental counter.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer:
One time at lunch, I had my shirt on inside out, and I hadn’t noticed. My cousin pointed out the exposed seams. At first I didn’t quite understand what they meant, but then I looked down at the shirt. The care label was showing beside my collar, too, so it wasn’t just one little thing out of place.

I felt embarrassed because it seemed so obvious once I knew. I kept thinking, “How did I put this on without noticing?” And then I wondered who else might have noticed before my cousin said anything. It was a small thing, really, but suddenly I felt very self-conscious about what I was wearing.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I felt proud of a serving bowl I made on the pottery wheel. It had blue glaze inside, and after firing, the rim was smooth. It was nice to look at it and think, I made that.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: The last meal I had was supper—pan-fried cod and boiled potatoes. My brother was sitting across the table from me. I put a squeeze of lemon over the fish.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: My car skidded on ice once, and I was really scared. The rear wheels were sliding toward a ditch, and there was a mailbox inches from my window. I remember how close it looked.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I remember finishing a crossword without any help for the first time. It was a Sunday puzzle with a science theme, and I penciled in the last answer over breakfast. I felt really pleased with myself. There’s something satisfying about working through a puzzle and realizing you’ve managed the whole thing on your own. That’s what stands out to me, more than the individual clues.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
answer: I had a bowl of rice porridge this morning, with sliced scallions stirred through it. It was breakfast before my early shift at the map shop, where I work as an assistant. I don’t remember much else about the meal—it was just breakfast before work.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: My niece surprised me with a visit on Sunday. I remember her bicycle leaning against the gate. It was lovely to have her there when I hadn’t been expecting her. We played backgammon together, and I just enjoyed her company. It wasn’t a big occasion, but I felt happy spending that time with her.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember a little girl dropping her ice cream. She still had the cone in her hand, but it was empty. That was the part that really got to me—she had the cone, but the thing she wanted was gone. I felt sorry for her, and I could do something about it, so I bought her a replacement scoop. It was a small thing to do, but it felt worth doing.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer:
“When my cat came home after being missing. I remember the muddy paw prints on the porch—such a small thing, but suddenly they were something to be happy about instead of something to clean up. And that familiar bell on the collar. It’s funny how a little sound can mean so much when you’ve been missing it.

I was just so glad the cat was home. There were the paws and the mud and the bell, all those ordinary things, and I wanted to take them all in. I like looking at the stars, and sometimes one little thing catches your attention and you keep looking. It was a bit like that, except this was right there on my porch. Mostly I remember that feeling of relief, not having to keep wondering where my cat was.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer:
There was a grass fire near my campsite. I remember the smell of smoke inside the tent—that’s the part that comes back most clearly. A tent doesn’t feel like much protection when you can smell smoke through it. And the flames were climbing the dry bank. The dryness really stood out to me then, watching the fire move up it.

I’m an amateur stargazer, so being out camping is usually something I associate with looking up, noticing what’s in the sky. But with the fire, my attention kept coming back to the bank and the tent, how close everything felt. I was afraid it would reach the campsite. I can’t give you a clear sequence of every moment, or say who was around me. What I remember is that smoke inside, and the flames going upward, and feeling that I couldn’t just settle back down and ignore it.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: One time I was bowling and took my turn out of order. The person who was supposed to go next was still choosing a ball, and I went ahead. I got a strike, too—but then it came up under the wrong name on the screen. That was the embarrassing part, looking up and realizing I’d just bowled somebody else’s turn. A strike is something you want your name next to, and there I was noticing the name only after I’d thrown the ball. Meanwhile, the person whose turn it actually was was still picking one out.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: There was a boy at the fair who’d lost his tickets. He showed me his empty pocket—it had a torn seam. I felt bad for him, so I gave him two of my ride coupons. I wanted him to still have a bit of fun.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: “Before each morning shift, I make tea to take with me. I use loose tea and brew it in a pot, then fill my thermos. That’s part of getting ready to go down to the kiosk I run on the ferry pier. I tuck the filled thermos beside an apple so they’re together when I pack up. Mostly I’m thinking about getting everything ready for the shift and making sure I haven’t left my tea behind.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember having supper with an exchange student who was missing home. He had a family photograph beside his plate. I felt for him and lent him my phone so he could call home. I just wanted him to feel a little less alone.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer:
“I felt proud when a poem I’d written was accepted by a magazine. They mailed me a copy of the issue, and seeing my name printed beneath the title really meant something to me. It was my poem, but there it was in a magazine, where someone else could read it.

I work as a cashier in a college cafeteria, and this was something different—something I’d made myself. What stays with me is seeing the title and then my name underneath. I’d written something that someone wanted to publish. I felt proud of that.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer: One time I was making pancake batter, and a rotten egg spoiled it. There was this watery, greenish liquid in the mixing bowl, and the sulfur smell spread throughout the kitchen. That’s what I remember most—the smell, along with the sight of that liquid in something I was making to eat. It was really disgusting. I couldn’t think of it as pancake batter anymore; it was just a bowl of something rotten.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: I felt happy when I found my lost wedding ring in the garden. There was a glint beneath the bench, and there it was. I looked at our wedding date engraved inside—it was such a relief to have it back.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I felt embarrassed at a family portrait session. I was wearing mismatched shoes—one black loafer and one brown. The photographer noticed while I was in a seated pose. There we were, having a family picture taken, and my shoes didn’t even match. That’s the part that sticks with me: having it noticed right when I was posing for the photograph.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: I felt sad on my last shift with a coworker who was retiring. I remember her unpinning her name tag from her apron, and the farewell card beside the till. It was strange thinking she wouldn’t be there anymore.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt sad?
answer: The first time I went fishing after my friend died was sad. His usual seat in the boat was empty, and his initials were still on the tackle box. I just kept noticing he wasn’t there.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer:
“I remember a birthday picnic my friends organized for me. There were paper lanterns above the picnic table and a lemon cake with candles. Those are the details that stand out when I think about it—the lanterns overhead and the cake there in front of me, with my friends around.

What made me happy was that they’d put it together for me. I remember thinking how nice it was to have people who wanted to celebrate with me. It wasn’t just having a birthday cake; it was feeling remembered and cared about. I felt really glad to be there with them.”

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d give directions to my usual post office, at 16 Palmer Road. From my home, you head south along Grove Street. When you get to the bank, turn left onto Palmer Road, then look for number 16. The bank is the landmark I’d tell someone to watch for so they know where to turn. I collect postage stamps, so the post office is a familiar place for me.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt embarrassed?
answer: I remember turning up for a dinner party a whole week early. The host answered the door in pajamas, and I realized something was wrong. I had the invitation in my pocket, with the date right there on it. I felt so foolish for not checking it properly. It was just an innocent mistake, but standing there, I wished I could disappear.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer:
I run a kiosk on a ferry pier, and I remember a delivery cyclist who was stranded there after dark. He had a flat tire on the rear wheel. What struck me was that he was working, and suddenly he couldn’t carry on. I thought how frustrating that would be—having deliveries to make and being stuck with your bike in the dark.

I had a work light at the kiosk, so I lent it to him. It wasn’t going to fix the tire, but at least he could see what he was dealing with. I felt sorry for him, and I wanted to do something useful rather than just stand there feeling sorry. That’s the part I remember most clearly: being able to offer a small thing when someone was having a difficult time.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer:
"I remember being inside a cave when my flashlight went out. The entrance was around a bend, so I couldn’t see it from where I was. That was what frightened me—not just the light going out, but not being able to look back and see the way out.

There was cold water dripping onto my shoulders. I work as a swimming pool caretaker, so water itself is familiar, but it felt very different in there. Each drip drew my attention back to how cold and dark it was. I kept thinking about that bend and where the entrance was. With the flashlight working, I hadn’t thought so much about needing to see it. Once it went out, that was all I wanted—to see where I was going."

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: “I felt really proud when a kite I’d made finally stayed up in the air. I was out by the dunes, and I’d made it a longer tail cut from an old sheet. What I remember most is watching it stay up and realizing it wasn’t coming straight back down. It stayed above the dunes for ten minutes. I’d made the thing myself, so seeing it actually fly was a lovely feeling. I just wanted to keep watching it.”

question: How would you give someone driving directions from your home to a place you go regularly?
answer: I’d tell them to head south from my home along Mill Street toward the rowing club. The clubhouse is on the left, opposite the boat ramp. I go there regularly for practice.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: “My first crop of strawberries on the balcony comes to mind. I had six ripe berries together in one bowl. Six doesn’t sound like a lot, but these were strawberries I’d grown, so that little bowl felt like a real achievement. And there were enough to share—I saved two for a neighbor. That was another nice part of it, having something I’d grown myself to give someone.”

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember a grass fire near my campsite. I could smell smoke inside the tent, and the flames were climbing the dry bank. That frightened me—how dry everything was. Usually I’m looking up at the stars, not watching the ground like that.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt compassion for someone?
answer: I remember being on a bus when someone was getting on in the sleet. They had a walker, and their bare hands were gripping the metal. I felt sorry for them, being out in that weather without anything covering their hands. I had a spare pair of mittens, so I offered them to the passenger. It was a small thing, but I wanted them to have some warmth.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt proud?
answer: I was proud of a bookcase I made from leftover pine. The top shelf came out level on the first try, which pleased me. And it held every cookbook—that was the best part, seeing them all fit.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: My niece surprised me with a visit on Sunday. I remember her bicycle leaning against the gate. We played backgammon, and it was just lovely spending time together.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: An old bandmate called me out of the blue. Hearing that familiar laugh felt really good. We made plans for lunch the following Saturday, and I was happy to have that to look forward to.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt disgusted?
answer:
I remember seeing a cockroach inside a bakery display case. That was bad enough, but then I noticed a second one underneath a pastry tray. What really disgusted me was watching one of them brush a glazed bun with its antennae. It was right there, touching something that someone was supposed to eat.

I couldn’t stop looking at that spot on the bun. The glaze had looked appetizing, and then suddenly all I could think about was the roach touching it and where else it might have been. Seeing the second one made it worse—it wasn’t just one insect passing through. I felt sick to my stomach, and I didn’t want anything from that case.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt afraid?
answer: I remember a small earthquake while I was having dinner. The overhead lamp was swinging sideways, and I could hear plates rattling inside the cupboard. It was frightening to have ordinary things suddenly moving around like that. That’s what stays with me most—the feeling that everything had become unsteady.

question: Can you tell me about a time when you felt happy?
answer: I remember seeing the first ducklings on the park pond. There were five of them following their mother, and I was watching them. What really caught my attention was the smallest one climbing onto a floating log. That’s the part I remember most clearly—that little duckling getting onto the log. It was such a small thing, but it made me happy. I enjoyed just watching them, especially that smallest one.

question: Can you describe what you usually do in the morning?
answer: Before breakfast I feed the sparrows. I scoop the sunflower seeds out of the tin for them, and I pour fresh water into the birdbath. That’s something I do every day. The water makes me think of work—I’m a swimming pool caretaker, so water is part of my day there too, though a birdbath is a different sort of thing. But you were asking about mornings. It’s the sparrows first, getting their seeds out and making sure there’s fresh water, and then I have my breakfast.

question: Can you tell me about the last meal you ate?
